_note: The proposals that are not about the deficit: two that move money in opposite directions, one that binds a spending line, and the one that makes the bloc act as a single power against the nations outside it. See docs/bloc-model.md. V4.5b sponsors and decision classes, placed by tools/council_probe.gd table T. cohesion_fund and recovery_facility are UNANIMITY: multiannual-budget and own-resources matters are, and the real recovery fund rode the Own Resources Decision through unanimity and national ratification. common_external_tariff stays qualified majority, because trade policy is. Under unanimity cohesion_fund's 0.28 call drew 26 vetoes at every cell of the sweep grid. The transfer term prices every member as a payer, and nobody draws on the fund, so no position could carry it. Under qualified majority it had never opened in a 168-month run either. It now calls 0.05, at (-0.4, 0.0), and its sponsor is POL, the plan's. CZE is the one veto. On 2026-10-15 the author ruled that a sponsor votes for its own proposal (orgs.gd _vote_of). Before that ruling, POL vetoed its own fund and PRT stood in for it. The seven V4.5b rows were placed by `--sweep`. defence_industry_fund (FRA) sits at (0.0, -0.4), the qualified-majority row inside the abstention window: France for carries it, 454 to 266; France abstaining carries it, 373 to 266; France against blocks it, 373 to 347. Six cells on the grid carry it alone, and that is not a design choice. carbon_border_adjustment, investment_floor, steel_safeguard, migration_solidarity_pact and cap_reform carry alone on EVERY cell, so their positions are flavour only. Each has a lobbying sponsor and costs a member little; the council does not need France for them, and that is the contrast with the window. enlargement_preaccession_fund is sponsored by POL. It vetoed its own proposal until the sponsor rule of 2026-10-15; it now votes for, and CZE is the one veto.

proposals.name: Cohesion Fund Expansion
proposals.summary: A larger common fund for the bloc's poorer regions, paid for by a higher call on every member's budget.

proposals.name: Recovery and Resilience Facility
proposals.summary: Joint borrowing against the bloc's own credit, disbursed to members as investment grants. Cheaper than borrowing alone, and it is the bloc's balance sheet that carries it.

proposals.name: Common External Tariff
proposals.summary: The bloc levies as one on goods entering from outside it. Every member's customs post charges the same rate, and no member sets its own.

proposals.name: Defence Industry Fund
proposals.summary: A common fund that buys European-made equipment for members' armed forces. The money is the bloc's; the factories it fills are mostly in the members that proposed it.

proposals.name: Carbon Border Adjustment
proposals.summary: Imports from outside the bloc pay at the border the carbon price its own producers already pay at home. Fair to the factories inside, a tariff to everyone outside.

proposals.name: Public Investment Floor
proposals.summary: Every member keeps infrastructure [g=spending]spending[/g] at or above 2.5% of GDP. The rule that reads the other way from the deficit rules: it is the cutting that breaches it.

proposals.name: Pre-Accession Fund
proposals.summary: Money to bring the candidate states up to the bloc's standards before they join. Paid now by the members, for a council that will be larger and harder to move later.

proposals.name: Steel Safeguard
proposals.summary: A quota-and-tariff wall around the bloc's steel market against cheap imports. The mills are saved; every member that builds anything out of steel pays for it.

proposals.name: Migration Solidarity Pact
proposals.summary: Every member either takes a share of the arrivals at the bloc's southern edge or pays into a fund that houses them. The frontline members get the money; the others get to choose which kind of help they give.

proposals.name: Farm Policy Reform
proposals.summary: The common farm budget is cut back and the savings returned to members' own budgets. Lighter calls for every treasury, and a hard year for every member whose farmers vote.
